## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trial results yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so the budget is tight and either seed luck or a poor inductive bias could explain it. The hard part of the task is working out where each brick lands. That layer is the maximum height under the footprint, and the move is right only when every footprint cell at that layer is 'missing' and nothing missing is left below it. The starting network squashes all layers together with 1x1 convs, so it has to learn to look things up by height. A per-layer ('2.5D') network sees each layer's build, target and missing cells as a stack relative to that layer, scores each placement at each layer, and then takes a soft maximum over layers. That fits the task better and costs about the same compute as the starting network (estimated r≈0.9). Training gives only 32 PPO updates by default, so the recipe also matters. This round is a 2x2 test (network × recipe) with the starting network and default recipe as the fourth cell.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and also 0 on training success in the last 10%. That holds for both networks and both recipes, so the 2x2 test told us nothing. Giving the starting network about 1.8x the samples and 3.7x the updates did not help. Nor did the strongly structured layer-wise network, which has no spatial context. One possible cause: the PoolHead and the layer-wise net hard-code where each brick's footprint sits relative to its anchor cell. If this world uses a different anchor or orientation (the task warns it may differ), only a learned spatial head can adapt. Also, an exact build needs every placement right plus a well-timed DONE, so the network probably needs more depth and receptive field. This round tests: a deeper residual conv net with a learned 3x3 per-brick head and the mask as an input, trained with two recipes (2 epochs, and 1 epoch with more samples); and the layer-wise net with added spatial context and mask inputs.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0, in both dev and training success, across three network families and several sample counts. So the network design alone is probably not the limit. My leading guess is that the policy collapses to pressing DONE. Early on, random placements mostly add extra cells and earn negative reward. DONE returns 0, which is far better than the expected return of more random play (about -1). Its advantage is therefore much larger than the small gain from the few correct placements. Once the policy presses DONE almost every time, it stops exploring, and train success stays at 0, which matches what we see. I can't confirm this from the logs, because they only report success rates. This round tests ways to stop the collapse: a higher entropy coefficient, a lower gamma (which shrinks DONE's advantage), and 1 PPO epoch for the most samples (about 426k at r≤1). I use the starting net at two entropy levels and the layer-wise net, whose structure best matches the rule for a correct placement.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0, both on dev and on the training success averaged over the last 10% of training. That covers three network families, recipes from 131k to 426k steps, entropy from 0.01 to 0.05 and gamma from 0.9 to 0.95, so the recipe and DONE-collapse do not explain the failure. Every network so far assumes that action (t, y, x) is spatially aligned with observation cell (y, x), because each scores placements locally: footprint pooling, layer-wise pooling, or a 3x3 head. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. If the action layout is not aligned with the observation grid (for example transposed or offset by more than one cell), all of these nets would fail in the same way, which is what we see. So the last round tests heads with learned global routing between observation and action positions: an MLP-Mixer, a conv trunk with a dense flattened action head, and a conv-plus-token-mixing hybrid. All three use the recipe that gives the most samples (1 epoch).
